title: Docker Fundamentals
subtitle: The mental model behind containers, images and registries
description: Start from zero and build a durable understanding of what Docker is, why it exists, and how images, containers and registries fit together. Every later course builds on these ideas.
outcomes: Explain the difference between a container and a virtual machine
Install and verify Docker Engine and Compose
Describe the image → container → registry relationship
Run, inspect and remove your first containers confidently

modules.title: The container model
modules.summary: Why containers exist and the three objects you use every day.

lessons.title: What Docker actually is
lessons.summary: Docker is packaging plus isolation: a portable filesystem and process model that runs the same way on your laptop and in production.
objectives: Define a container without marketing language
Identify the three core Docker objects

sections.title: A container is an isolated process
sections.body:
A container is not a tiny virtual machine. It is one or more Linux processes running on the host kernel, isolated with namespaces and constrained with cgroups. What makes it feel like a machine is the filesystem: the container sees its own root filesystem, built from an image.

That distinction explains most container behaviour. Containers start in milliseconds because no operating system boots. They share the host kernel, so a Linux container cannot run on a Windows kernel without a Linux VM underneath. And when the main process exits, the container exits — there is no init system by default keeping it alive.

sections.caption: The Docker client talks to a daemon, which uses containerd and runc to start isolated processes.

sections.title: Images, containers and registries
sections.body:
An **image** is an immutable, layered filesystem plus metadata such as the default command, environment and exposed ports. A **container** is a running (or stopped) instance of an image with a thin writable layer on top. A **registry** stores and distributes images by name and digest.

The relationship is one-directional: you build or pull an image, then create containers from it. Changes inside a container do not modify the image. To keep changes, commit them or — far better — update the Dockerfile and rebuild.

sections.title: The one-sentence version
sections.body: Docker gives a process a private filesystem and a predictable environment, then ships that filesystem as a versioned artifact you can run anywhere the engine runs.

exercises.title: Explain it back
exercises.prompt: In two sentences, explain why two containers can run different Node.js versions on the same host without conflict.
exercises.expected: Each image carries its own filesystem, including its own Node.js binary; the host kernel is shared but userland is not.

exercises.title: Identify the objects
exercises.prompt: You run `docker run -d nginx`. Name the image, the container, and where the image came from.
exercises.expected: Image: nginx:latest. Container: a new instance with a writable layer. Source: Docker Hub registry unless cached locally.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a container and a VM?
options: Containers share the host kernel; VMs run a full guest OS
questions.explain: Containers are isolated processes on the host kernel. VMs boot an entire guest operating system.

questions.question: Which object is immutable?
questions.explain: Images are immutable. Containers add a writable layer on top.

questions.question: A container stops when…
questions.explain: The container lifecycle is tied to PID 1 inside the container.

lessons.title: Install and verify Docker
lessons.summary: A working engine, a working Compose plugin, and the five commands that prove your installation is healthy.
objectives: Check that the client and daemon are both reachable
Read the output of docker version and docker info
Recognise the most common Linux permission problem

sections.title: Client and daemon are two programs
sections.body: `docker version` reports both halves of the system. The **Client** section is the CLI you just ran. The **Server** section is the daemon. If the client prints but the server section errors, Docker is installed but the engine is not running or your user cannot reach it.

sections.code:
docker version
docker info
docker compose version
docker run --rm hello-world
sections.output:
Client: Docker Engine 29.x
Server: Docker Engine 29.x
Docker Compose version v5.x

Hello from Docker!
This message shows that your installation appears to be working correctly.
sections.note: `hello-world` is the smallest useful smoke test: it pulls an image, creates a container, runs it, and exits.

sections.title: The permission problem
sections.body:
On Linux the daemon listens on a Unix socket owned by root. Adding your user to the `docker` group grants effective root-equivalent access:

```bash
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
```

Log out and back in for the group change to apply. Treat docker-group membership as root access — it is not a sandbox boundary. For stronger isolation, use rootless mode.

sections.title: Never expose the daemon over unauthenticated TCP
sections.body: A plain `tcp://0.0.0.0:2375` endpoint gives anyone who can reach it full control of the host. Use SSH contexts or mutual TLS instead.

items.title: Verify the engine
items.body: Run `docker info` and confirm the Server Version and Storage Driver are populated.

items.title: Verify Compose
items.body: Run `docker compose version`. Compose v2 is a plugin: `docker compose`, not `docker-compose`.

items.title: Run a smoke test
items.body: Run `docker run --rm hello-world` and confirm the exit message.

exercises.title: Health check
exercises.prompt: Run the three commands that prove client, daemon and Compose are healthy.
exercises.command: docker version && docker info --format "{{.ServerVersion}}" && docker compose version
exercises.expected: docker version, docker info, docker compose version all return server/plugin details.

exercises.title: Smoke test
exercises.prompt: Run hello-world without leaving a stopped container behind.
exercises.expected: The container runs and is removed automatically.

questions.question: docker version shows a Client section but the Server section fails. What is the most likely cause?
options: The daemon is not running or is not reachable
questions.explain: The CLI and daemon are separate; a missing Server section means the client cannot reach the engine.

questions.question: What does adding a user to the docker group effectively grant?
questions.explain: The daemon can mount host paths and start privileged containers, so socket access is root-equivalent.

questions.question: Which command proves Compose v2 is installed?
questions.explain: Compose v2 is invoked as a Docker CLI plugin: `docker compose version`.

lessons.title: Images, containers and registries
lessons.summary: How a name becomes a running process: tags, digests, pulls and the local image store.
objectives: Read an image reference such as nginx:1.27-alpine
Trace the pull → create → run path

sections.title: Anatomy of an image reference
sections.body:
A reference has up to four parts: `registry/repository:tag`. `nginx:1.27-alpine` uses Docker Hub, the official `nginx` repository and the `1.27-alpine` tag. `ghcr.io/acme/api:v2` uses the GitHub Container Registry. When the registry is omitted, Docker Hub is assumed.

A **tag** is a mutable pointer. A **digest** (`sha256:…`) is the immutable content identity. Production systems should pin digests when reproducibility matters, or at minimum use specific version tags rather than `latest`.

sections.code:
docker pull nginx:1.27-alpine
docker image ls nginx
docker image inspect nginx:1.27-alpine --format '{{.RepoDigests}}'
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27-alpine
docker ps
docker stop web && docker rm web
sections.output:
REPOSITORY   TAG            IMAGE ID       SIZE
nginx        1.27-alpine    a1b2c3d4e5f6   48.2MB
[nginx@sha256:9f1e...]

sections.caption: Each Dockerfile instruction that changes the filesystem adds a layer. Layers are shared between images.

sections.title: Pull is not always a download
sections.body: If the image and all layers already exist locally, `docker run` skips the pull. When layers are shared, only missing layers are downloaded. The writable container layer is always new and is deleted with the container unless you use a volume.

sections.title: Images are content-addressed
sections.body: The same layer is stored once even if ten images reference it. That is why `docker system df` can show a large shared size and a smaller unique size.

exercises.title: Read the reference
exercises.prompt: Decompose `registry.example.com/team/api:2.4.1` into registry, repository, and tag.

exercises.title: Pin a digest
exercises.prompt: Inspect nginx:1.27-alpine and copy its RepoDigest.
exercises.expected: The inspect output includes a RepoDigests entry with an immutable sha256 digest.

questions.question: In ghcr.io/acme/api:v2, what is the registry?
questions.explain: The first component is the registry host when it contains a dot.

questions.question: Which identifier is immutable?
questions.explain: Tags can be moved; a digest identifies exact content.

questions.question: When you delete a container, what happens to its writable layer?
options: It is removed with the container
It is stored in the registry
It moves to a volume automatically
questions.explain: The writable layer belongs to the container and is deleted with it. Use volumes for persistence.

lessons.title: The build → ship → run workflow
lessons.summary: The loop you will repeat for the rest of your career, from a Dockerfile in your editor to a running service.
objectives: Describe the build, ship and run phases
Know which artifact moves between environments

sections.title: Build once, run everywhere
sections.body:
The canonical workflow has three phases. **Build** turns a Dockerfile and build context into an image. **Ship** pushes that image to a registry. **Run** pulls the exact image and starts containers wherever it is needed.

The important discipline is that the same image moves through environments. Configuration — database URLs, feature flags, secrets — is injected at runtime as environment variables, mounted files or secret objects. Rebuilding for staging versus production destroys the guarantee you are testing the artifact you will deploy.

sections.code:
# 1. Build
docker build -t acme/api:1.4.0 .

# 2. Ship (tag + push)
docker tag acme/api:1.4.0 registry.example.com/team/api:1.4.0
docker push registry.example.com/team/api:1.4.0

# 3. Run
docker run -d --name api \
  -p 3000:3000 \
  -e NODE_ENV=production \
  -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://db:5432/app \
  registry.example.com/team/api:1.4.0
sections.note: In Compose the same phases are `docker compose build`, `docker compose push`, and `docker compose up -d`.

sections.caption: A registry is the hand-off point between build systems and runtime environments.

sections.title: Environment parity
sections.body: Use the same base image family across development and production. Alpine in production and Debian locally is a common source of subtle native-module differences.

exercises.title: Map the phases
exercises.prompt: For `docker compose up -d --build`, identify the build, ship and run parts.
exercises.expected: Build: --build. Ship: pull/push happens separately; Compose pulls missing images. Run: up -d creates containers.

exercises.title: Write the loop
exercises.prompt: Write the three commands that build, push, and run an image named app:v1 in a registry.
exercises.expected: docker build -t REGISTRY/app:v1 . ; docker push REGISTRY/app:v1 ; docker run -d REGISTRY/app:v1

questions.question: What should move from staging to production?
questions.explain: Deploy the identical image; configuration is injected at runtime.

questions.question: Which phase publishes an image?
questions.explain: Shipping means tagging and pushing to a registry.

questions.question: Where should database passwords live?
questions.explain: Secrets must never be in layers or build arguments that persist in image history.

lessons.title: Lab: your first container
lessons.summary: Run nginx, read its logs, exec into it, publish a port, and clean up without leaving a mess.
objectives: Run a detached container with a name and port mapping
Read logs and execute a command inside a container

sections.title: The exercise
sections.body: You will start an nginx web server, verify it over HTTP, inspect its logs, open a shell inside it, then remove everything. Use the integrated lab when Docker is available; the commands are identical to a normal terminal.

items.title: Start the server
items.body: Run nginx detached, give it the name `ops-web`, and publish host port 8080 to container port 80.

items.title: Verify
items.body: Request http://localhost:8080 and confirm the default nginx welcome page.

items.title: Observe
items.body: Read the last 50 log lines. Then run `hostname` inside the container.

items.title: Clean up
items.body: Stop and remove the container, then remove the image if it is not needed.

sections.code:
docker run -d --name ops-web -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine
curl -I http://localhost:8080
docker logs --tail 50 ops-web
docker exec -it ops-web hostname
docker stop ops-web
docker rm ops-web
sections.note: `docker exec` starts a second process in the container namespace. `hostname` returns the container id prefix by default.

sections.title: Stop is not remove
sections.body: A stopped container still exists and still holds its writable layer, name and port reservation. `docker ps` hides it; `docker ps -a` shows it. Remove with `docker rm` when finished.

exercises.title: Publish on loopback only
exercises.prompt: Start nginx so it is reachable on 127.0.0.1:8088, not on every interface.
exercises.expected: The port binding is restricted to loopback.

exercises.title: Find the PID
exercises.prompt: Use inspect to find the host PID of the container main process.

questions.question: What does -p 8080:80 mean?
options: Host port 8080 maps to container port 80

questions.question: Which command opens an interactive shell in a running container?
questions.explain: `docker exec` starts an additional process in a running container.

questions.question: Why does docker ps not show the container after docker stop?
options: docker ps shows running containers only
questions.explain: Use `docker ps -a` to include stopped containers.

lab.title: Run and inspect nginx
lab.brief: Complete the four steps using the lab terminal. The lab constrains resources and disables host mounts.

steps.instruction: Start nginx:alpine detached on port 8080 with the name ops-web.
List running containers and confirm the port mapping.
